# 124 · A partitioner rewritten with floorMod keeps every hash on a partition and moves every negative key

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | high | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`Partitioner#partitionFor`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its bit mask, is rewritten as `Math.floorMod(hash, n)`, which also lands every hash on a partition: the module's property still holds and the tests pass. The regression proof, run by the tool's own checker, finds that every negative hash now goes to a different partition than before. Half the keys of a topic move on deploy, and the records of such a key straddle two partitions.

Tags: [messaging](../README.md#tag-messaging), [numeric-code](../README.md#tag-numeric-code), [routing-change](../README.md#tag-routing-change), [own-checker](../README.md#tag-own-checker)

## The change

Replace `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions` with `Math.floorMod(hash, numPartitions)`: the remainder in the mathematical sense, never negative, so the mask is not needed and the method says what it computes. The check on the partition count stays. The tests pass unchanged: positive hashes spread as before, negative hashes land on a partition, a topic without partitions is refused.

**Before** ([`Partitioner.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java), line 9):

```java

    private Partitioner() {}

    /** Kafka's {@code Utils.toPositive(hash) % numPartitions}: clear the sign bit, then take the remainder. */
    public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
        if (numPartitions <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
        }
        return (hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java

    private Partitioner() {}

    /** The hash modulo the partition count, in the mathematical sense: never negative, whatever the sign of the hash. */
    public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
        if (numPartitions <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
        }
        return Math.floorMod(hash, numPartitions);
    }
}
```

<details><summary>Patch</summary>

```diff
--- a/examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java
+++ b/examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/Partitioner.java
@@ -9,11 +9,11 @@
 
     private Partitioner() {}
 
-    /** Kafka's {@code Utils.toPositive(hash) % numPartitions}: clear the sign bit, then take the remainder. */
+    /** The hash modulo the partition count, in the mathematical sense: never negative, whatever the sign of the hash. */
     public static int partitionFor(int hash, int numPartitions) {
         if (numPartitions <= 0) {
             throw new IllegalArgumentException("a topic has at least one partition");
         }
-        return (hash & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions;
+        return Math.floorMod(hash, numPartitions);
     }
 }
```

</details>

## What the verifier found

The two versions disagree. The prover found this input, and the verifier replayed it in jvmcontract's bytecode interpreter against both versions:

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `partitionFor(hash=-1, numPartitions=3)` | `1` | `2` |

One disagreeing input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `hash: int × numPartitions: int`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

Kafka's ordering guarantee is per partition, and a consumer, a Streams state store or a compacted topic rests on every record of a key landing on the same partition as the last. `floorMod` and the masked remainder agree on non-negative hashes and on little else: for a negative hash the mask adds 2^31 while `floorMod` adds a multiple of the partition count, and the two remainders differ unless the count divides 2^31. Half of all keys, those whose hash is negative, move to another partition the moment the new producer is deployed; during a rolling deploy the records of such a key go to two partitions at once, consumers see them out of order, a Streams application finds the key's state on another instance, and a compacted topic keeps two latest values for one key. Nothing fails: the property that every hash lands on a partition still holds, and the tests still pass.

## Why the verdict is right

The regression proof asks whether the two versions give the same partition for every hash and count, and the tool's own checker answers it: the harness is run symbolically path by path, the bundled SAT solver deciding at each branch which sides are feasible, and on the path where both versions return it is asked for a hash and a count on which the results differ. It looks in small ranges first, as JBMC is run: among hashes and counts in [0, 20] the versions agree, since the mask and `floorMod` are the same function on non-negative hashes; among values in [-100000, 100000] the solver finds a negative hash, and the interpreter shrinks it to `partitionFor(hash=-1, numPartitions=3)`: 1 before, 2 after. The staged search is what makes the witness readable, and the stage it was found in says that no non-negative hash is affected, which is the shape of the defect.

## What to do

Keep the mask, with a comment saying why it is not `floorMod` either: a partitioner's output is part of the topic's layout, and a change to it is a migration, not a cleanup. If the mathematical remainder is wanted, introduce it as a second partitioner class for new topics only, as Kafka's `partitioner.class` setting allows.

## Notes

- Checked by the tool's own bounded model checker (`approach.engine: native`, the tool's `--engine native`), not JBMC: the method is over two `int` parameters, with a remainder and `Math.floorMod`, both circuits the checker has. The library's run of this shape took 0.4 s: three paths, fifteen solver calls, the witness found in the second stage of the search as `partitionFor(hash=-85120, numPartitions=100000)` and shrunk to `(-1, 3)` in 87 interpreter runs. The measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.
- The checker's search is staged as JBMC's is (inputs in [0:20], then [-100000:100000], then everything), and the stage is reported: `searching inputs in [-100000:100000]` says that the first stage had no counterexample, so every non-negative hash keeps its partition. A path that fails only on large values does not end the search: the checker goes on through the remaining paths, for as long again as the first violation took, in case one of them fails in a smaller stage. Until this cycle the checker returned the first model the solver gave, which for three 64-bit values the shrinker did not bring down (example 122's second note).
- The module's property, `result >= 0 && result < numPartitions` for every `numPartitions > 0` (example 023), holds of `floorMod` as it does of the mask, so a property proof passes this change: the property says what every partitioner must do, not that this one does what it did. Regression verification is the check for a cleanup that is meant to change nothing. (The tool's own checker proves that property too, in 53 s: an unsatisfiability proof over a 32-bit remainder is where JBMC's single formula beats path-by-path exploration.)
- The disagreement is wide: `hash & 0x7fffffff` is `hash + 2^31` for a negative hash, so the two remainders agree on negative hashes only when the partition count divides 2^31, that is for a count that is a power of two. With 12 partitions, as the tests use, 2^31 leaves a remainder of 8, and every negative hash moves eight partitions along.
- Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by jvmcontract's own checker (CaDiCaL) in 0.1 s searching inputs in [-100000:100000] as partitionFor(hash=-100000, numPartitions=100000), shrunk to the input above in 85 interpreter runs, replayed in the interpreter; domain hash: int × numPartitions: int.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.

**Provenance:** Constructed on the partitioner kernel of example 023, whose `Math.abs` rewrite the property catches; this rewrite the property does not catch, and the regression proof does. The technique is regression verification run by the tool's own checker, with the staged search over inputs that JBMC's runs have.
